criteria.rationale: The delivered sample is a data-only module that consumes the kit through its public Presentation contract. It adds no rendering, animation, navigation or registration code of its own. The kit's registry discovers the module by glob, PresentationHost validates it and mounts the Viewer, and the Viewer resolves each step's scene and passes it to the shared Stage. This holds for the whole deck, since there is a single step module.

The product has no Talk/groupKey/layoutId API. Under INV-009's intent, the delivered design is one persistent Stage whose scene prop changes with the step, and Viewer never remounts it. Stable identity comes from the presentation-owned element ids. resolveScene keeps an element's id across steps, and Stage keys each rendered element by that id under AnimatePresence. Persisting elements therefore animate x, y, width, height and path in place.

Responsibilities are separated cleanly. The sample is pure data in src/presentations/<name>/index.ts. Registry, host, viewer, view-state, scene resolution, geometry, stage rendering and validation each live in their own src/presentation module. Browser verification lives under scripts/presentation-verify. The required presentation title input is consumed, not ignored, and I found no dead public contracts.

The requirement is an acceptable alternative, and its intent is that generated presentations make the current step visibly distinct in their navigation chrome. The delivered code meets that intent. In `src/presentation/Viewer.tsx`, each table-of-contents button carries the semantic `aria-current='step'` attribute on the current item and keeps the stable `psk-outline-item` class as its hook. The progress indicator shows `{view.step} / {stepCount}`. Prev/next buttons are disabled at the ends of the deck. In `src/presentation/presentation.css`, `.psk-outline-item[aria-current='step']` gets a distinct background and font weight, and `.psk-btn:disabled` is dimmed. That stylesheet is project-local CSS in the repo, with every rule scoped under `.psk-*`. No external package or remote embed supplies it. The sample presentation module is pure data with no styling. Judge C ruled fail for two reasons. First, the kit's own `presentation.css` and the `COLORS` in `Stage.tsx` supply default colors, fonts, borders and button styles. That is true, but the 'kit stays free of defaults' clause is part of the mechanism the quotes describe, and this criterion's intent takes precedence over that mechanism. Here the viewer chrome is project-local source that the skill copies into the project. Its styling sits in local scoped CSS, not in a remote theme, so that design still meets the intent. Second, the viewer renders no attribution. The intent does not ask for attribution, and the guidance says the demo need not inject one. A legibility failure can't rest on an element the candidate never renders. Neither reason shows the stated intent unmet. Judges A and B are borne out by the cited lines.

Neither the delivered sample nor the shared presentation boundary adds any export, editor or hosting/publishing feature. The registry only discovers local modules, PresentationHost only lists and serves them, and Viewer offers just step and mode controls. Verification is objective: DOM geometry, step indicator, console and page errors, and teleport sampling. It does not score taste. Demo-specific content stays in its own module, and the shared mechanisms are not duplicated.

The Step model has only `caption` and `changes`. It has no stable id, no section/era label and no separate one-line presenter title, so the requirement for a stable identity, a section label and two narration texts is unmet.

Visible on-screen step numbers are derived from step position. The controls render `{view.step} / {stepCount}`, where `view.step` is the one-based position in the steps array. Browse mode also renders `{i + 1}. {step.caption}` for each step, using the array index. Both are visible text, not aria or data attributes.

The typed boundary (`Presentation`, `Step`, `Change`, `SceneElement`) does not carry a stable step id or a section/era label. Those are the quoted requirement for this criterion. Step identity exists only as array position.

Each entity is rendered with `key={element.id}`, so an element with the same id keeps its React and motion identity across steps. `initial` applies only on mount. `animate` drives x/y, rect width/height, connector path `d` and label position, with a 0.6s transition, so a persisting entity animates in place from its old state to its new state.

The kit has no per-step remount transition. A single persistent Stage receives the resolved scene, and entities are keyed by id inside `AnimatePresence` in default sync mode, so incoming and outgoing entities coexist. A persisting entity is not removed and remounted, and it is not given a delayed or hidden entrance. It stays visible while animating.

A newcomer's entry has no delay. `placed()` gives newcomers `initial:{opacity:0}`, `animate:{opacity:1}` and the same `transitionFor(false)` (0.6s, no `delay`) used by the persisting entities' x/y/size motion. Connectors and labels fade in the same way. Nothing holds a newcomer until persisting entities settle, so entry starts at the same time as the layout motion.

The kit renders every authored entity layer (groups, connectors, nodes/text, highlights) through `AnimatePresence`. Body, highlight and connector elements declare `exit:{opacity:0}`, so an entity removed in a later step stays rendered while it fades out. With reduced motion it is removed immediately by design.

All steps share one persistent Stage instance. Navigation changes only the `scene` prop, derived by `resolveScene`, and the Stage is never remounted between steps. Successive diagram states therefore update the existing scene instead of rebuilding it.

Continuing entities keep their stable key, so the mounted motion nodes do not replay `initial`. A label's fade is keyed by its text lines, so an unchanged label is not re-faded, and only a changed label re-keys. Entities morph through animated props rather than being re-introduced as newcomers.

The kit supports only declarative JSON elements placed on a grid. It exposes no way to use raw motion elements with authored layoutIds, and no author-facing className or style hooks on primitives. Per-step literal coordinates and custom elements are not supported.

Steps have no one-line title. Present mode renders only the stage and the controls row (`n / N` indicator, prev/next, toggle). It shows no step title, and the prev/next controls are visible rather than hidden.

Browse mode renders a caption, prev/next controls, an `n / N` indicator and a step outline (a side panel on viewports of at least 900px). It does not render the active step's own title, because steps have no title. The panel's `psk-title` is the presentation title, so the required active-step title is absent.
The viewer switches between present and browse at runtime, through a toggle button and the `p` key. `reduceView` for `toggle` only flips `mode` and spreads the existing state, so `step` is unchanged.
`keyAction` maps ArrowRight, PageDown and Space to next, and ArrowLeft and PageUp to prev. The Viewer registers a window keydown listener that dispatches the action.

Non-mouse pointer down and up on the stage record the horizontal delta, and `classifySwipe` maps dx<0 (swipe left) to next and dx>0 (swipe right) to prev, with a 50px threshold, dispatching a single-step action.

On-screen and keyboard navigation controls are provided. The browse outline has a button per step that dispatches `goto` with that step, and Home/End jump to first and last. `goto` is clamped to range.

The navigation entries that stand for steps are the browse-mode outline buttons (the table of contents). The button for the active step gets aria-current="step", and no other button does. That is semantic current-step state. The same attribute is the stable hook that presentation CSS targets to style the active entry. The progress indicator is a single text counter ({view.step} / {stepCount}), not a row of per-step items. It shows the current position as visible text, which is the current-step information itself, so there is no set of items in which one would need an active-state attribute. A focused test checks that exactly one aria-current="step" appears and that it sits on the active step's entry. Judge B's reason is that the progress span has no current-step attribute. The code bears out that observation, but it does not decide the requirement. The intent asks for current-state semantics on any applicable navigation controls. The counter is not a control and does not represent one step among several. The position it reports is visible to every viewer and to assistive technology as its text. So judges A and C's pass verdict holds.

`keyAction` guards form fields (INPUT, TEXTAREA, SELECT) and contentEditable. For buttons and links it exempts only Space. ArrowRight, ArrowLeft, PageDown and PageUp are still mapped to next/prev and `preventDefault()`ed even when a rendered button (prev/next/mode/outline) has focus. Those step-navigation keys therefore move the deck while a button is focused, rather than being left to the control.
`reduceView` clamps every step change to [1, stepCount] with no wrap-around. `prev` at step 1 stays at 1, and the prev button is disabled at step 1.
`next` is clamped to `stepCount`, so advancing on the last step stays on the last step with no wrap. The next button is disabled at the end.

The diagram is an SVG with a fixed `viewBox` of 880×380. `fitScale` is `min(w/CANVAS_W, h/CANVAS_H)`, a single factor applied to both width and height. The `w`/`h` inputs are measured by ResizeObserver from the stage element that actually contains the SVG, so the canvas stays within the stage area. The stage is sized differently for present (flex area above the controls) and browse (aspect-ratio box on narrow viewports, flex beside a 320px panel on wide ones), so the fit geometry is per mode.

The kit defines a fixed composition area of 880×380 units (22×10 grid of 40×38 cells). The rendered Stage consumes those values for its `viewBox` and fit scale, so all composition happens on a fixed canvas that is scaled uniformly.

The kit does expose `psk-*` classes and `data-*` attributes. However, visual choices (colors, typography, borders, button styling, spacing) come from the kit itself, not from the presentation or host. This breaks the quoted requirement that those choices come from the presentation or host app. Presentations are pure data and cannot supply styling.

The kit's output is not left unstyled for the presentation or host to style. It ships default colors, fonts, borders, button styles and shadows-free but themed visuals through `presentation.css` and the inline `COLORS` palette. The stage's SVG fills and strokes are hardcoded and are not exposed for override.

Elements are placed only by named grid cell (`at`, `span`) through fixed element types. The kit has no author-facing path for raw motion elements with stable `layoutId`s, and no class/style props on primitives for literal coordinates. The coordinate-heavy diagram scenario is therefore not supported.

The kit renders no attribution link at all, so there is no default link to the and-scene repository (https://github.com/Codagent-AI/and-scene). I covered every component the kit exports. PresentationHost renders only a presentation list (a heading and `<a className="psk-link" href="?presentation=…">` links to the user's own presentations), the ProblemsView or the Viewer. PresentationGate renders either its children or the Host. A search of all of src and of the template copy for github, attribution, and-scene, brand, logo and powered found no attribution element. The only `github.com` match anywhere in the source was none outside package-lock.json, which I excluded. The one `<a>` in the kit is a presentation-list link, not an attribution. The criterion expects a default attribution link that targets the and-scene repo, and the source has none.

The kit has no attribution element, so it exposes no stable class or data hook for an attribution that presentation-owned or host CSS could target to restyle, reposition or hide it. The kit's hooks are the `psk-*` classes and `data-*` attributes on the list, viewer, problems and stage chrome. None of them marks an attribution, because no attribution is rendered in Host, Gate, Viewer, Stage, ProblemsView or ErrorBoundary. The kit therefore does not meet the requirement for an attribution styling hook.

The kit renders no brand mark when the host supplies none. I checked all the kit's top-level rendered components: PresentationGate renders only children or the Host. PresentationHost renders a plain 'Presentations' list heading, a not-found notice, ProblemsView or the Viewer. A search of src/ and the template copy for brand, logo, powered and and-scene found no logo, image, wordmark or product name rendered by the kit. The only title text rendered comes from the presentation's own data, such as `presentation.title` and `p.title`.

The requirement is that gathering covers the topic, the visual style, and the content of each step. SKILL.md step 2 asks only for the topic, plus audience, depth, key points and length. It never establishes or derives a visual style. The kit's look is fixed in the kit's CSS. Step 2 also batches all the missing questions into one message.

The requirement is that the user can build after giving only some details, with no hard completeness gate. SKILL.md step 2 says 'Do not assume a missing detail even when the topic is clear. Generate nothing until the user answers.' That is a hard gate. The only escape is the user explicitly delegating. The workflow also has no iteration or modify path after generation.

I agree with judges A and C. SKILL.md step 2 (lines 23-30) has the skill ask only about details the user has not given: audience, depth or scope, key points and length. It says to ask about 'exactly those ... and no others' and 'Do not ask for anything the request already states.' So a complete prompt produces no questions, and the workflow goes straight through naming (step 3), bootstrap (step 4), writing (step 5), verification (step 6) and the report (step 7, lines 31-70). The only pause in those steps is a name collision. The user can build with partial detail, and there is no hard completeness gate. The topic is the only thing the skill insists on (lines 24-25). Visual style and per-step content are never asked for; the skill derives them from the authoring rules (lines 45-57). For any of the four optional details the user can reply 'you decide', and the skill picks a value and says which one it chose (line 30). So the user controls how much to specify and can build after giving only a topic. Iteration is supported: running the skill again on an existing slug triggers the replace-or-rename question (lines 31-33), and the rules allow replacing an existing presentation once the user confirms (line 74). The user can therefore revise a generated presentation. Judge B's fail rests on line 29, 'Generate nothing until the user answers'. That sentence only applies to questions the skill has actually asked. Lines 26-28 limit questions to missing details and forbid asking for anything already stated, so a complete prompt produces no question and there is nothing to wait for. For a complete prompt, line 29 is therefore not a gate and does not contradict the bypass. B's reason does not show any clause of the requirement unmet.

In an empty directory or a project with no anchors, the skill must do a full scaffold of build setup, scene kit and presentation index, and install all dependencies. SKILL.md step 1 and bootstrap.ts refuse anything without vite, react and typescript in package.json ('unsupported', nothing changed). The skill never creates the build setup. Only motion, lucide-react, playwright and @types/node are added, so the eslint stack and the base dependencies are never installed.

The requirement is contract-level detection of the three anchors, skipping scaffolding when all are present, with cosmetic differences not triggering a re-scaffold. bootstrap.ts keys on a byte-identical match with the template. A kit that differs in any file makes it refuse ('differs', exit 1), and a project with a working equivalent setup is not recognised. It does not model the three anchors or resolve where infrastructure belongs.

The skill copies only the missing template files and leaves identical existing ones alone. It does not scaffold missing anchors as the fixture defines them. It never creates the build setup, and no presentation-index scaffolding exists beyond the host's glob. Any differing existing kit file aborts the entire bootstrap instead of the skill filling in only what is missing.

The guidance credits a scaffold that defines no default presentation colors, fonts, button styles, borders or similar. The bootstrapped kit stylesheet defines them. It sets a white background, slate and blue colors, a system font stack, bordered and rounded button styles and a highlighted outline item. The bootstrap also does not install the full dependency set: the eslint stack is never added and react, vite and typescript are assumed present.

SKILL.md directs running `node <this skill's directory>/bootstrap.ts <project root>`. bootstrap.ts computes TEMPLATE_DIR from its own file location (`dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))` joined with `template`), so templates resolve from the skill directory, not the working directory. A sync script and drift tests keep the snapshot aligned with the canonical `src/presentation` kit.

The requirement is that for a non-empty project lacking the kit, the skill states the target location it will scaffold into and proceeds only after the user confirms. SKILL.md has no target-resolution step and no monorepo handling. It runs bootstrap against `<project root>` directly with no stated target and no confirmation.

SKILL.md has no instruction to state the target location for a standalone non-empty project and wait for the user's confirmation before scaffolding. Bootstrap runs unconditionally at step 4. The only confirmation rule covers replacing existing files, not scaffolding into a project.

The guidance fails this when no instruction requires stating the scaffold target and waiting for confirmation before scaffolding a non-empty project. No such instruction exists. Step 4 installs the kit, edits package.json, .gitignore and src/main.tsx, and runs the package install without asking the user first.

A new presentation is written as its own folder, `src/presentations/<slug>/index.ts`. The registry discovers every `../presentations/*/index.ts` through `import.meta.glob`, so it is registered with no manual step. It is reachable at `?presentation=<slug>`, which the report step gives as the link. The skill creates browser presentations from a topic.

The requirement is that a presentation's designed visual look lives in files owned by the presentation or the host app, not in the reusable kit. Presentations are data-only modules that use `import type` and a fixed primitive set. The skill has no mechanism or instruction for presentation-owned or host-owned styling. All visuals come from the kit's own stylesheet.

Creating a new presentation leaves existing ones intact and reachable. Step 3 checks whether `src/presentations/<slug>` exists and changes nothing until the user answers. Rules forbid replacing existing presentation or kit files without confirmation. The glob registry picks up every folder, so existing presentations stay listed and reachable alongside the new one.

The guidance requires explicit instructions that resolve an ambiguous modification target before editing. SKILL.md has no modify flow at all. It covers only creating a new presentation from a topic and handles slug collisions, with nothing about choosing among existing presentations to modify.

The guidance requires explicit instructions that confine edits to the chosen presentation. SKILL.md has no modification workflow and no rule limiting edits to a single chosen presentation. Its only scoping rule is not to edit the shared kit.

SKILL.md step 6 requires `npx tsc -b --noEmit`, lint, `npm run build` and `npm run verify:presentations` before step 7. Step 7 allows a success report 'Only when every check passes'. The verify command renders every presentation in a real browser at several viewport sizes in both modes. browser.ts shows it loads every step (step 1 to the last) in each viewport and mode. It records console errors and page errors and fails on them. It also runs browser-based composition checks: horizontal overflow, diagram or controls outside the viewport, label collision, clipped labels, labels too small, and scene geometry, and it takes screenshots of failures. VIEWPORTS includes 360x640, so a narrow viewport is always checked. That covers the build, the first-step render with no errors, the visual composition check of the first, last and dense steps, and the narrow viewport. Judge B says no visual composition inspection exists. The material shows otherwise: the instructed verify command does a browser composition check on every step, so B's reason does not decide the requirement.

The requirement says that when a check fails, the skill fixes the issue itself and re-checks. The review guidance says to fail when the instructions 'name a failure type that may be reported instead of fixed'. SKILL.md step 6 has the general fix-and-re-run rule, but it then names one failure mode of the render-verification tool: the verification browser is not installed. For that case it tells the agent to 'report that verification could not run and give the install hint `npx playwright install chromium`'. The agent does not install Chromium itself and re-run the checks. That is a named failure type that is reported instead of fixed, so the 'fixes the issues itself and re-checks' part of the requirement is not met for it. Judges A and C note that success is still not reported in that case. That is true, but it meets only the 'does not report success' part. The guidance makes a reported-instead-of-fixed failure type decisive, so their reason does not make this a pass. Judge B's reason is borne out by the cited lines, and it decides the criterion.

Nothing in the verifier asserts that the reference sample is present, registered, or matches the outline. discoverPresentations returns [] when src/presentations is missing or empty. verifyPresentations then runs no per-presentation checks, and makeReport sets ok to true when no result failed. The snapshot check only compares kit files against the template and does not look at the sample. A project with no sample would pass instead of failing at a sample or build phase. The sample is only checked by a vitest unit test (sample.test.ts), which is not part of the verify command.

Preview binding, port reservation and browser URLs all use the 127.0.0.1 loopback address. The verifier builds the project, serves it with vite.preview, and drives real Chromium through every step of each presentation.

The preview is started in-process with vite.preview on a port the verifier reserved itself, with strictPort. If a stale server held the port, vite would throw instead of silently reusing it. Readiness is the awaited vite.preview promise, not HTTP polling of a reused port, so the verifier cannot mistake a stale listener for its own server. The preview is closed in a finally block, so it is cleaned up on both passing and failing runs.

I rule pass, siding with judges A and C. Source: checkCombo listens for console errors and uncaught page errors (browser.ts:150-151). It drains them into the current step's problems in observe() (browser.ts:187), or records leftovers at the last step reached (browser.ts:248). record() stamps each one with the step (browser.ts:167). RENDERING_CODES puts console-error and page-error under the 'rendering' check (browser.ts:109-112, 170). index.ts:107-108 marks a check 'failed' when it has failures. makeReport sets ok=false when any check is failed (report.ts:4). verify-presentations.ts:8 then sets exit code 1, and formatReport/formatFailure print `step: N` (report.ts:8-23). Executable evidence: the int-004 console-error and page-error tests inject the fault with a mutation (mutations/index.ts:65-76). Each asserts `failedChecks(report,'healthy')` equals ['rendering'], and that the failure has the matching code and step 1 (int-004:147-165). failedChecks is defined at int-004:15-16 on top of statusOf (helpers.ts:113-114). So the assertion is literally that the rendering check's status is 'failed'. Through report.ts:4 and verify-presentations.ts:8, a failed check is exactly what forces ok=false and exit code 1. The test therefore establishes the non-zero exit outcome and the offending step. Judge B said no browser-error test asserts a command exit. That is true, but it does not decide the criterion: the guidance asks for a test asserting a non-zero exit and the step. Here the asserted failed status maps directly to exit 1 through a single unconditional line, with no branch in between. The CLI path that prints the step and exits non-zero is itself exercised end to end in e2e-002:40-48.

A step that renders wrongly or fails to advance fails verification, and the failure names the step. Absent values are not treated as progress. collectObservation parses the indicator as `match ? Number(match[1]) : null`, and evaluateScene compares `obs.step !== expected.step`, so an unreadable indicator (null) yields 'wrong-step' rather than matching step 1. There is no Number(null) coercion. The step count comes from `data.steps.length` in the validated data, not from the page, so an unreadable page count cannot make the loops step through nothing and pass. A failed click or navigation in checkCombo is caught and recorded as 'navigation-failed' at `at.step`. Every failure marks its check failed, which leads to ok=false and exit 1. int-004's stale-scene test asserts report.ok false and a 'wrong-scene' failure at step 2 on the forward route; the no-transition test asserts a teleport at step 2. Judge B's points do not decide the requirement. (1) The missing CLI exit assertion: the asserted `report.ok === false` maps directly to exitCode 1 (verify-presentations.ts:8), and e2e-002 runs that CLI path. (2) checkTransitions' catch has no step field: the same forward Next-step clicks are first driven by checkCombo, whose catch records the step. B points to no produced scenario where only the animated pass fails, and the guidance names none.

No project-local helper captures a screenshot of every step for visual review. The only screenshots are failure evidence that the verifier takes for a step that already has problems. There is no npm script, command, or SKILL.md instruction for a per-step capture helper.

There is no screenshot helper that enumerates every step and writes an image per step to a project-local artifact directory. Screenshots exist only for failures. No test asserts one screenshot per step.

There is no per-step screenshot helper with a settle interval before each capture. The verifier does wait for `data-settled` before observing a step, but its screenshots are taken only on failure and are not a per-step capture helper with a configured settle interval. The requirement for a screenshot helper that waits before each capture is not met.

No screenshot helper prints advisory overlap warnings for visible text or chrome. The overlap-like checks are failures, not warnings: data-level overlap in validate.ts and label-collision in evaluateRendering. They cover element labels only, not chrome such as progress dots or controls. No test builds an unmarked collision and asserts a helper warning, and no skill instructions tell the reader to review such warnings.

There is no screenshot helper that supports marking an overlapping subtree as allowed. No allow-overlap hook is implemented in the verifier, and no test marks a subtree and asserts that no warning is reported for it.

No helper compares the rendered styles of the active step indicator with the inactive ones. The browser checks never read computed styles of progress or table-of-contents entries, there is no active-state warning output, and no focused test exists.

No screenshot helper emits warnings that identify elements by visible text, accessible name, hook, or selector. Failures from the verifier name elements by scene element id, but there is no advisory warning output for overlap or chrome-polish, and no focused test asserts an attribution warning.

criteria.rationale: Both the repository and template copies of verify start the preview through Vite's preview() API and close it in a finally block that every exit after the preview starts passes through: success, a failed check, and a thrown error. If the browser fails to launch, the function returns before any preview exists. No npm or npx wrapper hosts the preview. No inspect script is delivered (a grep for 'inspect' finds only SKILL.md prose and the sample), so verify is the only script that starts a preview. I rule A and B's pass. Judge C's reason is that no inspect script was delivered. That absence is scored under the inspect and diagnostics criteria. It does not show any delivered preview being left running, which is the only thing this criterion checks.

Verify awaits `npm run build` to completion and returns on failure before it calls vite.preview(). Readiness is the awaited preview() API call, which resolves once the server is listening and rejects on a port clash because strictPort is set. Nothing parses printed output: logLevel is silent. So the ANSI and split-chunk parsing clause does not apply, as the guidance states for a preview() API call. Every browser wait on the served page has an explicit timeout: waitForSelector 5000 ms, waitSettled 4000 or 1500 ms, click 3000 ms. I rule A and B's pass. Judge C's reason is that vite.preview() has no timeout wrapper. But that call is not a polling wait for printed readiness: it settles when listen() succeeds or fails. The guidance names a preview() call that resolves with its address as a valid readiness mechanism, so C's reason does not show an unbounded readiness wait.

The skill's bootstrap template verify tooling meets all three clauses. (1) It verifies every registered presentation. The CLI takes only an optional project directory (verify-presentations.ts:5). discoverPresentations lists every src/presentations/<dir>/index.ts (discover.ts:15-34). checkData keeps every valid one (data.ts:7-22). runBrowserChecks loops over every viewport, mode and presentation (browser.ts:328-349). Nothing is a hardcoded route or a first-entry pick. (2) No unregistered slug can time out or be accepted through the landing-page fallback, because the template never takes a slug. Each route it drives is built from a discovered id (browser.ts:155, 261). checkDiscovery reads the built host's rendered [data-presentation-id] list and compares it with the directory ids using compareIds (observation.ts:276-283). Any missing or extra id becomes a discovery-mismatch failure with a clear message (browser.ts:120-139). index.ts:104 records that failure, makeReport sets ok=false when any check failed (report.ts:3-5), and verify-presentations.ts:8 then sets exitCode 1. (3) The template has no sample-specific content. Every module in the template verify tree is quoted in full: the entry points, index, discover, data, types, browser, observation, report and snapshot. They contain only generic defaults: the viewport and mode matrix, label-size and tolerance constants, and generic button names such as 'Next step' and 'Previous step'. Captions, ids, step counts and element text all come from each discovered presentation's data, through expectedFor (observation.ts:69-80) and data.steps. Snapshot paths point at the skill's template layout, not the sample. Judge C's fail rests on the missing slug-validation entry point. The requirement accepts 'verify every registered route' in place of a slug argument, and with no slug input there is no slug path to time out or fall back to the landing page. Unregistered content is still rejected with a non-zero exit through the discovery mismatch. So C's stated reason does not show any clause unmet. My verdict agrees with Judges A and B.

No inspect helper was delivered. The repository and the skill template contain only verify-presentations and its presentation-verify modules. A grep for 'inspect' finds it only in prose and in a sample element id. None of the three required behaviours exist: rejecting a missing, zero or non-numeric step count or index; confirming the reported step index before each capture; and never succeeding with zero captures. The verify code does detect step problems through its observation loop, but this criterion judges the inspect helper only.

The verification checks read the rendered page at every step. collectObservation reads the step indicator, the [data-caption] text and visibility, each [data-element-id] label, the controls and the root text from the live DOM. observe() compares these with the expected values at every step on the reload, forward, backward and outline passes. The outline pass navigates by clicking the rendered numbered outline buttons. Registration is checked by reading the rendered [data-presentation-id] list. Presentation data is loaded by importing the modules, and no regex runs over source text. I rule A and B's pass. Judge C's reason is that the title and the full outline order are not collected. That concerns which elements a check reads, not regex matching over source text, which is the only fail condition this criterion names.

The criterion scores visual inspection diagnostics on every captured step, with captures that include the presentation's chrome. No visual inspection helper is delivered. SKILL.md's workflow lists only tsc, lint, build and verify:presentations. A grep for 'inspect' finds no script, and verify takes a screenshot only when a step already has failures: record() returns early when partials is empty. So no capture of each step exists for diagnostics to cover. I rule C's fail. Judges A and B relied on verify's per-step assertions and failure-only screenshots. The source audit already found that those screenshots happen only on failure and that no inspect helper captures steps. A and B's material therefore does not establish the visual inspection captures and diagnostics this criterion requires.

The only things the skill materializes are the kit snapshot files, which bootstrap.ts copies to the same relative paths in the target project. The presentation itself is authored per authoring.md, and no step or inspect templates exist. Relative imports in the template verification modules (`../../src/presentation/...`) resolve to the bootstrapped src/presentation. `presentation.css` is imported from the same directory as PresentationHost, and tsconfig.presentation.json is shipped to the project root. tests/int-001-bootstrap.test.ts bootstraps a scratch app from the isolated skill, runs the project build, and then runs verifyPresentations, which type-checks the tooling with tsconfig.presentation.json.

The description is third person ('Turns a topic into...') and says when to use the skill ('Use when asked to make, create or generate a presentation, explainer or walkthrough...'). It does not quote any example user phrases. The words after 'Use when' are a paraphrase, not quoted trigger phrases, so the quoted-phrases requirement (at least two) is unmet.

SKILL.md has no out-of-scope section. Its only sections are Workflow and Rules. It names none of PowerPoint or Keynote output, PDF or image export, a visual editor, or hosting, and so gives no redirect for any of them. A grep of the skill's markdown files for these terms found nothing relevant.

Step 7 tells the agent to report success with the link `?presentation=<slug>` only when every check passes. It defines no report template. It does not ask for the files changed, the build, render and inspect results, or the advisory warnings that remain, so the report's contents are largely undefined.

No presentation owns a stylesheet. The sample presentation is a TypeScript data module, and presentations are authored as src/presentations/<slug>/index.ts. The only stylesheet is the kit's host-owned presentation.css, and every selector in it is scoped under a `.psk-*` class. tests/scripts/css-scope.test.ts asserts that. Nothing leaks to other presentations after client-side navigation.

The kit's public exports are PresentationGate and PresentationHost. Both type their props explicitly ({children: ReactNode; search?: string} and HostProps {registry?, search?}), not as an untyped bag. Neither spreads caller props onto a DOM element, so a caller cannot override any identity hook. The internal Stage sets data-element-id, data-type and similar hooks from scene data, with no caller spread. Kit-only props such as registry and search are consumed in code and not forwarded to the DOM. Record<string, unknown> appears only in validate.ts's internal Loose type and in a local variable in resolve.ts. I rule A and B's pass. Judge C's reason is that the scene element types are data interfaces rather than rendered-element props. Scene records are data that the kit maps field by field, not components that take element props, and C admits the renderer controls identity attributes and does not forward records. None of the criterion's fail conditions applies: no untyped bag, no caller override of identity hooks, no kit-only prop forwarded.

The browser tests sleep for fixed times in two places. Many other assertions read state straight after an action instead of polling. The two fixed sleeps are enough to fail the requirement that no browser test uses a fixed sleep.

Tests that start a preview use `vite.preview` with `port: 0`, so the operating system assigns the port and no two test files share a fixed port. Browsers and previews are closed in afterAll or finally blocks. Child processes are started only with spawnSync (build, bootstrap, git), which waits for the process to exit. There is no npm or npx wrapper hiding a server. cleanup.test.ts checks that the port stops listening after close.

Round 0 treated every approved scenario in the three specs as floor coverage. Each scenario has a row with the public-surface action (real skill runs, bootstrap CLI, Chromium viewer journeys, verifier CLI) and an observed outcome. Round 1 re-ran the two fixed seams (bootstrap through symlinks, return-flow authoring) at the final revision. The scenarios the environment did not allow are disclosed with the reason: 'Validator fails on a bad presentation' and part of 'Existing checks unchanged', because the acceptance workflow forbids the Validator, tests and lint. I compared the log's scenario rows against the spec scenario headings and found no undisclosed omission.

The exploration log records what was done and what was seen for each scenario claim: the action, the exit codes, measured values (360×155.45, 13.1px, y 358.55→482.91, 880×380 before the observer fires) and the reported error codes. The round-1 claims are backed by two screenshots, a recorded TS error excerpt and the correction of it, and a before/after symlink log (old guard exit 0 silent; fixed guard refusal and exit 1). The 'build succeeded' fact is also given. Many named scratch files are not in the packet, but the log's own observations are specific enough for a reviewer to tell what was done and what happened. The screenshots carry metadata with a recorded observation (text equivalent) for each.

The recorded tested revision, c885ceeccb9b911dde2d5edf5d8f43efef92f255, is the same as the delivered commit in readiness.json, so there are no product changes after the last tested revision. The round-1 pass was scoped to the diff from ead28ff, which the log says resolves in the repository. The diff is four files across two seams. bootstrap.ts was explored by running the real CLI canonically and through file and directory symlinks. SKILL.md and authoring.md were explored by a real authoring-skill run. The changed bootstrap.test.ts was not run, and the record states the acceptance workflow forbids test suites, so it counts as explored.

The record discloses its gaps and limits. The Validator, test suites and lint were not run. Current-head CI is absent, and the CodeRabbit status is not project CI. chrome-devtools-axi was unavailable, so Playwright was used. The agent replies were scripted and the faults were scratch-only injections. The wait-ci tooling failure and the first-attempt typecheck failure are attributed. Non-npm package managers, other browsers and performance were not exercised. One unresolved decision (the initial 880×380 canvas frame) is carried forward. The completion claims ('READY for human acceptance', F-01 and F-02 resolved) match the evidence: the screenshots and the before/after log agree with what is claimed. I did not find a claim that overstates the evidence.

The ledger records many spec ambiguities with the requirement, a ruling and a rationale. The consequential ones are the attempt count, swipe direction, sample provenance, lint when absent, name collision versus bootstrap writes, off-canvas highlights, dedup identity and style isolation. The ledger also records the open first-frame sizing question, and the round-0 and round-1 findings, F-01 and F-02. The log and handoff disclose what was not run: the Validator, tests, lint, CI and non-Chromium browsers. I found no observed deviation that was left unrecorded.

The record keeps what it ran apart from what it inferred, and it misstates no fact. The style-isolation ruling says it rests on reading the CSS, not on running a browser. The F-02 instruction fix says it could not be re-tested in that round, and round 1 then re-tested it with a real skill run. The handoff says the Vitest assertions were inspected but not run, and that the Validator, tests and lint were not run. The two defects reproduced in natural runs, F-01 and F-02, were classified as defects, fixed, and re-tested. Judge C fails this criterion on the first-frame sizing case, but the cited material does not support that reason. The workflow saw an 880×380 canvas in a 360×155 stage only after it deliberately delayed the ResizeObserver callback by 1000ms (log line 118). The ledger and the log both say this isolates the sizing seam and does not show how long, or whether, the natural first frame is visible (ledger 259, log 136). So the run did not reproduce a violation of the "Small phone" scenario in the product's own behavior. It is a surfaced gap, framed as an open question. Calling it "not a clear defect under the approved wording" is a hedged judgment that matches that unknown, not a misstated fact. The record also did not omit or dismiss the case: it surfaced it, recorded the raw observation, and named the consequence of each option. The guidance says this framing must not fail the criterion.

The workflow settles questions that the approved definition answers, and records 'Decision pending: None' with a rationale for each. It names where the user's authority would be needed: a rightward swipe doing nothing, a recorded skill run as the sample's provenance, and a first-class return connector. Where a ruling found the code short of the definition, it treated that as something to fix, not as acceptable. Examples are style isolation, highlight canvas bounds, and the collision check before bootstrap writes. F-01 and F-02 were fixed and re-tested. Only the first-frame sizing case is escalated, with two options and the consequence of each: a briefly clipped frame, or a delayed first render. Judge C fails this criterion because the record offers to accept a reproduced violation. The material shows the clipped frame was seen only under an artificial 1000ms observer delay, and the record says natural visibility is unknown (log 118 and 136, ledger 259). So no reproduced violation is being classified as acceptable. The guidance allows a gap surfaced without reproduction to be put to the user as a decision, including accepting it, when the record states that option's consequence, and handoff line 47 does so. The workflow took no decision without authority. It left this one to the user.

The handoff names the one unresolved decision by subject, 'Initial small-phone canvas while ResizeObserver is pending', which matches the ledger heading. It does so in the Decision brief and again under 'Assumptions and material limitations'. It gives both options and the consequence of each, names the evidence file, adds the method's limit, and links acceptance-assumptions.md. It also keeps the material limitations the acceptance record identifies elsewhere: CI is absent; the Validator, tests and lint were not run; Vitest assertions were inspected but not run; non-npm package managers, other browsers and performance were not tested; and the sample's provenance cannot be shown. It also lists 17 implementation risks, each with its coverage status. Judge C fails this criterion because the handoff omits the console-error attribution gap (ledger 215-221). That ledger entry is an implementation-stage ruling marked 'Decision pending: None'. It tells the code to attribute console and page errors to their step, and is neither an unresolved decision nor an acceptance limitation. The acceptance log and findings never list it as remaining. The delivered verifier now drains errors 'attributed to the step being observed' and screenshots that state (source/scripts/presentation-verify/browser.ts:148-151, which is not citable here). So the handoff leaves out no unresolved decision or open limitation that the record identifies.
